chapter: Shows, scripts and the Mosby-era names
title: Clarence Muse, the Beaux Arts Theatre and the streetcar strike
summary: Muse helped seek backers, but the show was funded by a few friends; it opened at the Beaux Arts in 1946 and failed during a streetcar strike.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Mmmm hmmm. Okay, I see. And then you pulled out this copy of Ebony from...
That's the same thing in rehearsal.
Let's see, the date on the Ebony is April, 1946, and there's a picture of you with Clarence Muse.
Yeah.
And it says, "CO-PRODUCERS 'Reb' Spikes and

SPIKES - 181
Reel 5
Page 32

Clarence Muse run over script revisions of their show. Muse is a well-known Hollywood film actor." And you were telling me that it was your show, and Muse was just someone you asked to...to be a backer?

Well, Muse was trying to get me a produ...somebody to produce it. That's the way he got in on it, and he finally...when we done the show, he wasn't nowhere around, 'cause we done it ourself. We-- four or five of us--put in...some other friends around there put in a few hundred dollars, and we put the show on ourselves.
So it opened here at the Beaux Arts Theatre...
Beaux Art, yeah.
...which was...uh, toward downtown...
Eighth and...Eighth Street somewhere...
Eighth and Beacon. Here it is, yeah. And it opened in, what, 1946 was it?

Yeah, same thing, yeah. I'll tell you, we had a nice show...done that bug number in there with 'em all dancin' and it was a sensation, see? But the two weeks we's there was when the Los Angeles... uh...streetcar strike was, and by the time the strike was over, we were broke. 'Cause the Actors Guild made you...made us pay 'em so much a week, you know, and the people couldn't get there. People, they...everybody didn't have a car like they do now, you know. And the audience wasn't big enough for us to...after two weeks, we were broke.
What a shame! When was that, about? Was it the early part of '46?
I don't know what date it was now in '46.

'Cause, well, it hadn't opened yet when this Sentinel came out. The Sentinel...
Well, that was during rehearsal--same as in the book there. That's same as rehearsal.
So it was like toward the middle to late in '46...
Well, maybe two, three weeks before this. When was this? See here, February...no, it doesn't say on here, does it?
I don't think there's a date on there.
Well, you got the date of the paper there.
Well, yeah, but it hadn't opened yet then. That was January, and the Ebony is April.
Well, you see, we rehearsed three or four months up there 'cause a lot of these people were workin' people that was in the show, and we could only rehearse at night. See?
